title: Voiced K ゛— ガ ギ グ ゲ ゴ

points.name: ガ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as が — 'ga'; voiced version of カ
points.explanation: ガ makes the same 'ga' sound as hiragana が — voiced 'g' before 'ah', like in 'garden'. It's カ plus the dakuten (゛). Just as you learned in the hiragana chapters, the two small strokes at the top-right of a katakana character voice its consonant. ガ appears in ガイド (guide), ガラス (glass — from Portuguese 'vidro', but now used as ガラス in Japanese), and ガソリン (gasoline). ガラス is interesting because it came into Japanese from Dutch 'glas' during Japan's Edo period trading with the Netherlands.
rules: ガ = カ + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'ah'.
Same principle as hiragana — the dakuten voices any consonant in both scripts.
ガラス (glass) is from Dutch 'glas' — a reminder of Japan's early European trade history.
points.flashcardAnswer: ga — voiced version of カ; like the 'ga' in 'garden'

points.name: ギ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぎ — 'gi'; voiced version of キ
points.explanation: ギ makes the same 'gi' sound as hiragana ぎ — voiced 'g' before 'ee', like in 'give'. It's キ plus the dakuten. ギ appears in ギター (guitar — one of the most iconic loanwords), ギリシャ (Greece — from a Portuguese-derived rendering), and the combination ギャ (gya), which appears in words like ギャップ (gap) and ギャラ (fee for an appearance/performance). ギター is a wonderful example because the Japanese sound 'gitaa' is one beat longer than English 'guitar' (the long vowel ー stretches the 'a').
rules: ギ = キ + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'ee'.
ギター (guitar) is one of the most common musical instrument loanwords in Japanese.
Small ギャ (gya) creates combination sounds: ギャップ (gap), ギャラリー (gallery).
points.flashcardAnswer: gi — voiced version of キ; like 'gi' in 'give'

points.name: グ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ぐ — 'gu'; voiced version of ク
points.explanation: グ makes the same 'gu' sound as hiragana ぐ — voiced 'g' before the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'. It's ク plus the dakuten. グ appears in グループ (group), グローバル (global), and グラス (glass — the drinking vessel, as opposed to ガラス which is the material). Interestingly, Japanese has both ガラス (glass material) and グラス (drinking glass) as separate words from the same English root, used in different contexts. グローバル is a very commonly used buzzword in Japanese business contexts.
rules: グ = ク + dakuten; voiced 'g' before flat Japanese 'u'.
グループ (group) is extensively used in school, business, and social contexts.
グラス (drinking glass) vs ガラス (glass material) — same root, two separate loanwords!
points.flashcardAnswer: gu — voiced version of ク; like 'gu' in 'good'

points.name: ゲ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as げ — 'ge'; voiced version of ケ
points.explanation: ゲ makes the same 'ge' sound as hiragana げ — voiced 'g' before 'eh', like in 'get'. It's ケ plus the dakuten. ゲ appears in ゲーム (game), ゲスト (guest), and ゲート (gate). ゲーム is one of Japan's most important cultural and economic exports — the Japanese gaming industry (ゲーム産業[さんぎょう]) is world-class, and you'll encounter ゲーム everywhere from arcades (ゲームセンター) to home consoles. Japan is the birthplace of companies like Nintendo, Sony PlayStation, and Sega.
rules: ゲ = ケ + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'eh'.
ゲーム (game) is hugely important — Japan's gaming culture is world-famous.
ゲームセンター (game center / arcade) is a distinctly Japanese cultural institution.
points.flashcardAnswer: ge — voiced version of ケ; like 'ge' in 'get'

points.name: ゴ
points.shortDescription: Same sound as ご — 'go'; voiced version of コ
points.explanation: ゴ makes the same 'go' sound as hiragana ご — voiced 'g' before 'oh', simply sounding like the English word 'go'. It's コ plus the dakuten. ゴ appears in ゴール (goal), ゴリラ (gorilla), and ゴム (rubber / eraser — from Dutch 'gom'). ゴール is extremely useful for sports vocabulary. ゴリラ is one of those fun animal names that is an obvious loanword. And ゴム (rubber) is another Dutch-origin word from Japan's Edo period — ゴム消[け]し (gomu-keshi, rubber eraser) is the standard word for 'eraser' that every student in Japan uses daily.
rules: ゴ = コ + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'oh'.
ゴール (goal) is essential sports vocabulary.
ゴム (rubber/eraser) is from Dutch 'gom' — and ゴム消[け]し (eraser) is standard school vocabulary.
points.flashcardAnswer: go — voiced version of コ; sounds just like the English word 'go'

chapterPractice.prompt: What does the dakuten (゛) do to a katakana character?
chapterPractice.explanation: The dakuten (゛) voices the consonant — your vocal cords vibrate. カ (ka, no buzz) → ガ (ga, buzz). This is identical to how dakuten works in hiragana. The same two small strokes, the same voicing effect.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which katakana is the voiced version of ケ?
chapterPractice.explanation: ゲ is the voiced version of ケ. Add dakuten to ケ → ゲ. The 'ke' sound becomes 'ge' (as in 'get'). ゲーム (game) is the most famous word using ゲ.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ゲーム (geemu) means 'game'. ゲ (ge) + ー (long e) + ム (mu) = geemu. Japan is a gaming superpower — Nintendo, Sony, Sega, Capcom, and many others are Japanese companies.

chapterPractice.prompt: What does this katakana word mean?
chapterPractice.explanation: ギター (gitaa) means 'guitar'. ギ (gi) + ター (taa) = gitaa. Notice how the 'ar' at the end of English 'guitar' becomes the long vowel ー in Japanese — a very common pattern with 'r'-ending English words.
